And, the slight but noticeable delay between pushing the up or down frequency button and when it really locks on and you get sound again

Had this radio been really sensitive and really pulled in the distant stations or really done a great job on SW-SSB i would have forced myself to deal with the controls. So, i sent it back. Amazon was great and took it with my description of the problems. Perhaps they have taken some back before. SONY...ARE YOU LISTENING??

text_fidelity_a:
Magellan RoadMate 1470 4.7-Inch Widescreen Portable GPS Navigator I've been a Magellan user for several years - have owned four of their GPS systems, and always appreciate how they have improved their products. This unit is my 5th, and replaces a Magellan 4040. After using it for a while I've confident in saying this is the best one yet!

The most visible change is the actual size of the unit. The screen size has been increased, but the unit is thinner and lighter. Very sleek appearance, and the screen is a real joy -- sharp, clear graphics even in the sun, and bigger on-screen buttons for easy use. The mounting system has also been streamlined, and looks and works well. It mounts very easily on a NavMat holder (basically a bean-bag system that I got on Amazon. I'm a huge Navmat fan - makes it a snap to hide the GPS with narry a trace. Best accessory by far for any GPS).

The power connector was not well thought out, however. You have to connect it to the GPS unit AFTER you mount it in the holder. They should have moved the connector it a wee bit to the side to avoid that.

The only button is a slide-type power button on the top. Boot-up time is OK -- not speedy, but not a huge delay either. It does not have a "sleep" mode, so you have to do a cold boot every time. Not a problem in real world use - by the time you get situated in your car, the unit is ready to go.

Voice is clear and easy to understand. Not as natural sounding as a TomTom, but understandable.

Pretty much any recent GPS unit will get you where you want to go. I've found the routing on the Magellans to be very similar to Garmins - could be because they both use the same mapping set (Navteq). The Magellan shines, however, in features that I find helpful. The direction of the next turn is always visible regardless of how far away the next turn will be. Up until recently, Garmin did not offer this (they do now on some of their units). Sounds like a small issue, but I find it very helpful. The Magellan also allows you to very easily exclude a route (or portion). That's a fairly standard feature nowadays, but Magellan allows you to do it in a snap.

In terms of routing, Magellan offers four options (fastest, shortest, most use of freeways and least use). You can see all four options on the map (as a summary) at the same time so you can pick the best one for your needs. Perfect!!

Love the AAA Guidebook, which is a unique Magellan feature. Lets you get details about restaurants and other points of interest just like the paper version from AAA. I used it a lot in my 4040, especially when traveling out of town.

Other unique Magellan features I appreciate is the "ding dong" sound right before a turn (incredibly accurate!) and the fact that the software reminds you to "stay on the current road" when you encounter major exits. Some find that to be nagging, but it has saved me from inadvertently exiting on more than one occasion.

A new feature for Magellan is the lane guidance. Very nicely done. I've used this feature on Navigon units, and found it rather unhelpful. Magellan's implementation is far more useful, with better, clearer graphics. However, lane guidance is not available for every road.

The software is also nicely done - very logical to use. If you're a past Magellan user you can pick this up and use it in a second. If not, there's a short printed user's guide in the box (plus a CD-ROM with more in-depth info) that gets you up to speed quickly. The box also includes the mount, power connector for the car, and a USB cable. It does not include an AC adapter.

OK, now for the bad news. When it comes to customer service, Magellan has been horrid. We're talking so bad it's almost funny. I'm hoping this situation will change - the company was bought by Mitac late last year, and perhaps this will signal a change for the better in terms of customer support. Lord knows, they couldn't get any worse.

The leader, in my opinion, for customer support is Garmin. They are nice to deal with on the phone, answer emails promptly, and offer regular firmware updates. Whenever I buy a GPS as a gift I always buy Garmin since I don't want to saddle the recipient with the miserable service that Magellan offers. It's a shame, since Magellan offers some real benefits over Garmin, and more value for the money. Tom Tom is also decent when it comes to support, but they use TeleAtlas maps which are less complete than NavTeq (sp?).

Bottom line -- if you're looking for a straightforward GPS at a good price, this should be on your short list. It lacks features such as Bluetooth and an MP3 player, but for me, I want a GPS to offer guidance and not entertainment. This has a very robust feature set, great screen, and well-designed software. It also has traffic capabilities -- did not test that feature out, so I can't comment on it.

The "safe" bet continues to be Garmin. You'll pay a bit more, and get less features, but you can be assured of solid support. Whether Magellan's new owners will put them back on the right track (if you'll excuse the horrid, but unavoidable pun) in terms of customer service is not yet clear. I hope so -- they make a great product!

UPDATE: 5/21/09 There's a firmware update on the Magellan site. No new functionality (in terms of new features) but, according to the release notes it improves overall performance. Easy to install - just follow the included step-by-step instructions. It seems like it makes the unit a bit faster, but that could just be my imagination.
text_fidelity_b: Magellan RoadMate 1470 4.7-Inch Widescreen Portable GPS Navigator

FULLJA WiFi Digital Picture Frame - 10.1 Inch Smart Digital Photo Frame with FHD IPS Touch Screen, 32GB Memory, Motion Sensor WiFi Electronic Picture Frame Share Photos and Videos Via App Email I don’t love it. This seems overpriced for what you get. For the price, I was expecting it to look more like a photo frame but instead, it kinda feels like an old monitor. My goal was to hang it on the wall during art shows with process videos playing. It will work OK for that but I’m disappointed that unless the video is in the exact proportion of the frame, it will always look a little “off” and there’s no means of changing how it’s framed in the display.

I think it’s at its best without the clock or any other additions.

The pros: It really does work right out of the box. It only took minutes to get photos onto it. The big screen is nice, I can see details in my photos. It is also bright with vivid colors. I like that it is flat which is why it performs better than an average monitor as a picture frame. The simple black frame doesn’t detract from its appearance. I like that there is an app and my husband and I were able to add photos, and I also like that there is a way to add photos via card in case software changes make the app obsolete. With the app, I was able to get videos onto it in minutes. I also like that it has a large amount of storage space and the means to expand it..

The cons: It is slow. I didn’t love the way the photos are displayed. I also hate the default animations because they are a bit cheesy. I want it to fade or some other non-intrusive way to change photos, and there is no means to edit it. The features are incredibly barebones. I hate that the default includes the time etc, I just want it to look like a photo frame! The audio is a bit tinny, much more so than a television etc. I also find it bizarre in 2023 to have an item that warns that it can destroy a USB if it’s removed without turning it off first…that seems like such an old-school problem!

I wish the plug was white because the black looks bad against the wall, and I prefer a minimalist look.

For the price, I feel like this could be better. There are just so few options for customizing the display.

text_fidelity_a:
Echo Dot (2nd Generation) - Smart speaker with Alexa - White I've had my two Echo Dots for one year now. Now, a year later, Google Home has really come forward by leaps and bounds while Alexa has basically stayed exactly the same. For Android users, the easiest way to describe it is that the Alexa has become an iPhone vs. Google's Android. I think I am the norm in that there is almost no "Skill" I have use for with Alexa. Instead I ask things that are already built in features: weather, time, set alarm, add things to shopping list, and of course, control home devices like lights. However, ALL home devices can do those things just as easily and intuitively as Alexa does, so to see if you are getting the best device you need to compare other features:

Asking a question - Google wins hands down. Google uses... Google, to get your answer. Alexa uses Bing I think, nuff said. Most of the time the response from my Dot is "I'm sorry, I don't know that" and if it does "know", it is giving an answer to something I'm not truly asking. For example, I asked it what movies were playing on FOX tonight and the response was "I'm still learning about fox. Ask me a fox fact so I can learn more about them." Many times it even just answers to search the internet. Well, if I have to search the internet then I want to use Google to do it and there is no way to set your search engine. Essentially every time it tells me to search the internet, what I hear in my mind is "Use Google" - yeah, I think I just might, Amazon.

"Skills" apps - all but useless for every day life. Skills I can see some possibility of using are the reading a bedtime story if you have kids, or asking Alexa to play a game. But for adult life and for truly being a life/home assistant to you, none of the Skills compare at all to the platform that Google already has in place from decades of being an internet powerhouse. Example: finding your phone. This is a pretty common issue that I think it's reasonable to assume any of these home assist devices should be able to tackle easily. For Alexa you must download a "Skill" (there are a few to choose from) and register your phone number to that app. The major flaws with Alexa doing this are: 1. you need to first tell Alexa to open and use the skill with precise wording for it to work (i.e. "Alexa find my phone" won't work. "Alexa have Tracker find my phone" won't work. "Alexa open the Tracker app. Alexa have Tracker find my phone" won't work. "Alexa open the Tracker app. Alexa ask the Tracker app to find my phone" works). 2. if your ringer is off there is no ability to turn it on for the purpose of finding the phone. Essentially you'd be better off to add "me" to contacts with your own number and just tell Alexa "call me" because that is all you are getting with Alexa's "Skills", it's easier to just do that, and it only has the same flaw of not ringing if ringer is off. In comparison, with Google you download nothing, simply say "Google find my phone", and viola, your phone will ring whether the ringer is on or not. Google also has "Maps" which is huge. "Maps" gives you locations, hours of operation, can list like-businesses, tell you how to get somewhere and how long it will take you, and even tell you which buses to take if you have public transit in your area, etc. Alexa can only utilize Yelp and if a business isn't on Yelp then Alexa has no access to even the very basic info Yelp supplies (hours).

There's one 'Pro' to Echo over any other home device, and that is as it relates to other Amazon devices. Like Google, Amazon is also an internet powerhouse in it's own way. Having a Prime membership is the norm rather than the exception in most households, and obviously that means asking Echo to order something or play a Prime movie or Prime music is going to be smooth and easy with the Echo. Also, where Amazon still leads the pack is with it's Fire Stick, and again, obviously, Echo is going to be well integrated with that device, while other Home Assistants aren't given that level of access to integrate as well. So that's why I give it 2 stars - because I can't use my FireStick AS EASILY if I owned something other than an Echo. But I can still use the remote so that ability is def not worth more than two stars, especially when Google has the ability to take away access to things like YouTube (which it did) from Amazon in retaliation for being denied access to things like FireStick integration into it's own device.

Bottom line, Echo/Alexa seems great until you see how much better the later competitors to the market have improved on the user experience and are continuing to improve by leaps and bounds with each new update, while Amazon rests on 'we were the first'. Or, in other words, don't fall for yet another same ol' iPhone that is introducing features Android users have had for at least five years when instead you could just buy the Android and have the newest and best features right now.
text_fidelity_b: Echo Dot (2nd Generation) - Smart speaker with Alexa - White

(Old Model) WD Green 500GB Desktop Hard Drive: 3.5-inch, SATA 6 Gb/s, IntelliPower, 64MB Cache WD5000AZRX The only thing to be aware of is that Windows 8 has some difficulty recognizing the 3 gig partition, even on the 64 bit. If this is your second drive, you can use diskpart to get access to the full 3 gig -- just keep in mind this will erase your entire hard drive. Use it carefully. If it's your primary, your best bet is to partition it before you install Windows. If you aren't very technical, and just need a replacement drive, you're better off picking up a 2 TB, which is the biggest Win 8 can recognize without such additional configuration.

The drive itself is perfect. It's fast. It's quiet. It's reliable--I work in IT, and I've found WD drives over all to cause the fewest problems. This one has been put through some very heavy use with no issues.

HP Wireless Elite Keyboard v2 ...if you don't have a wrist rest or pad already, I highly recommend that you get one at the same time you get this keyboard. I was introduced to the chiclet- or scissor-style keyboard because of using one at work (using an Apple wired keyboard with an Intel Mac), and I have to say that I prefer it in every way to the more traditional keyboards. It is much quieter, and, for me, the feedback is pleasant. One thing I did not take into account, though, is that I had a wrist rest at work. So when I got this keyboard for home use and started using it, I loved it immediately--until the day I used it for hours on end. Then--ouch! My wrists began to ache.

Overall, this is a great keyboard. It connected to my computer without a problem, and the only lag in keystrokes I have experienced has been when the computer had just been "awakened" from sleep mode. For reasons I will not go into here, I am using this keyboard with a laptop: the laptop keyboard's lights indicate whether or not I have Caps Lock or Num Lock engaged on the wireless keyboard. I understand that won't help people using this keyboard with a desktop computer, but thought I'd put it out there anyway.

My conclusion: if you're a fan of the scissor-style keyboard and you have or are willing to invest in a wrist rest, you will enjoy this keyboard.
text_fidelity_b: HP Wireless Elite Keyboard v2
